stem: A male infant is diagnosed with inherited hemophilia A. Which pathophysiologic finding should the nurse associate with this disorder?

options.A: A low level of clotting factor VIII that impairs normal clot formation and increases bleeding risk
options.B: A low level of clotting factor IX, which defines hemophilia B rather than hemophilia A
options.C: Excess production of clotting factor VIII that primarily causes pathologic thrombosis
options.D: An isolated increase in platelet count that prevents prolonged bleeding after injury or surgery

rationale: CDC states that hemophilia is a bleeding disorder in which blood does not clot properly and that hemophilia A is caused by a lack or low level of clotting factor VIII. Therefore A is correct. Low factor IX defines hemophilia B, so B is incorrect. C reverses the factor abnormality and bleeding phenotype. D does not describe the defining clotting-factor defect of hemophilia A.
educational_objective: Associate inherited hemophilia A with low factor VIII activity and impaired clot formation that can cause spontaneous or prolonged bleeding.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: About Hemophilia; How Hemophilia Is Inherited
source_version_date: About Hemophilia dated 2025-03-05; inheritance page current and rechecked 2026-08-17
source_locator: About Hemophilia > Overview and Types: blood does not clot properly; hemophilia A is caused by lack/low level of factor VIII and hemophilia B by lack/low level of factor IX. How Hemophilia Is Inherited > Types of hemophilia and X chromosome inheritance
source_claim_supported: Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by low clotting factor VIII; hemophilia B is caused by low factor IX, and the common inherited forms are X-linked.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.15/PDF p.19: Apply knowledge of pathophysiology to client care; Recognize and report changes in client condition; Provide care for clients with acute and chronic health conditions
correction_summary: Replaced the nonauthoritative National Hemophilia Foundation homepage citation with current CDC primary guidance. Removed the family-member narrative and weak precaution claims, and rebuilt the item around the exact defining distinction between hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency). Difficulty reduced from hard to easy.

audit_findings.option_B: Wrong but highly plausible — factor IX deficiency is the corresponding defect in hemophilia B.
audit_findings.option_C: Wrong — reverses the direction of the factor abnormality and clinical phenotype.
audit_findings.option_D: Wrong — does not describe the clotting-factor deficiency that defines hemophilia A.
